report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. text.text: Multilingual children's language environments vary widely, yet they are often described by exposure proportions alone.

In this exploratory paper, we describe how caregivers distribute and combine languages in speech during a child-directed picturebook narration task, using language-use visualizations, language proportions, language entropy, proportion of multilingual utterances, span entropy, and memory.
We applied these measures to 146 narrations from caregivers in Singapore of children aged 0;8 to 3;4 and compared them to caregiver reports.

Caregivers reported and used different linguistic varieties with their children, and reported language use and observed language-use during narrations showed moderate correspondence, indicating they characterise different facets of multilingual input.

Among multilingual narrations, caregivers of older children used their languages less evenly and proportionally more English, whereas utterance-level mixing and span organisation showed no detectable age differences.
We discuss methodological considerations, including segmentation and labelling decisions and provide code for researchers to compute these measures.
Multilingual children vary in the languages they hear, how much they hear, and who provides that exposure (de Bree et al., 2017; Cychosz et al., 2021).

text.text: Caregivers also differ in whether they use more than one language within an interaction, often described as language mixing (Byers-Heinlein, 2013).

text.text: Characterising children's multilingual language experiences therefore requires considering not only which languages and how much, but also how caregivers use and combine languages (De Bruin, 2019; Arredondo & Castro, 2026).

text.text: Parental reports commonly estimate caregiver language patterns, mixing frequency, and relative exposure (for a review, Kašćelan et al., 2022).

text.text: They provide breadth across contexts, but limited information about how caregivers use their linguistic repertoires within an interaction (de Bruin et al., 2019; Arredondo & Castro, 2026).

text.text: Recordings complement parental reports by measuring speech directly, revealing differences among families with similar self-reported language-use proportions (Marchman et al., 2017; Orena et al., 2020), and actual child-directed language mixing (Bail et al., 2015; Kremin et al., 2022).

text.text: Typical recording-based measures also summarise multilingual input into language proportions, rather than moment-to-moment dynamic language mixing.

For example, a caregiver with 8:20 split between their languages might use each language in long, unbroken stretches, or they might deploy resources from both of their languages in a more blended way.
Multilingual speech is thus an unfolding sequence of caregiver language resource choices, not merely a mixture in different quantities.
Given that infants are sensitive to sequential regularities in speech (Saffran & Kirkham, 2018), how languages unfold in caregiver speech may matter in ways that broad comparisons miss.

text.text: In this report, we explore how a variety of approaches capture the ways that caregivers dynamically deploy resources from their languages.

Many existing approaches to multilingual data focus on the type or position of 'switches' between named languages (Code-mixing: Muysken, 2000 , Code-switching: Poplack, 1980) or assume that one language provides a grammatical frame for within which a switch can be observed (Matrix Language Framework: Myers-Scotton, 1997).
text.formatted: Many existing approaches to multilingual data focus on the type or position of 'switches' between named languages (Code-mixing: <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">Muysken, 2000</ref> <ref type="bibr">, Code-switching: Poplack, 1980)</ref> or assume that one language provides a grammatical frame for within which a switch can be observed <ref type="bibr">(Matrix Language Framework: Myers-Scotton, 1997)</ref>.

text.text: By contrast, alternative models focus on how linguistic resources are distributed and sequenced across an interaction without assuming that one language supplies a grammatical frame (Translanguaging: Garcia & Li, 2014; Polylanguaging: Ag & Jørgensen, 2013).
text.formatted: By contrast, alternative models focus on how linguistic resources are distributed and sequenced across an interaction without assuming that one language supplies a grammatical frame <ref type="bibr">(Translanguaging: Garcia & Li, 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Polylanguaging: Ag & Jørgensen, 2013)</ref>.

text.text: These newer approaches are better suited to majority-multilingual contexts where speakers draw on multiple linguistic resources in their speech.

In Singapore, speakers use linguistic resources primarily from English, Mandarin, Malay and Tamil (Leimgruber, 2012; Styles et al., 2022), alongside a rich shared vocabulary of lexical items from many language backgrounds (Tay, 1989; Alsagoff, 2010), often making code-switching models difficult to apply (Lee, 2003; Ong et al., 2013).

text.text: The current report documents translanguaging behaviour in 146 Singaporean parentchild dyads.
Caregivers reported their language use at home and narrated a wordless picture book to their child (0;8 to 3;4 years) over Zoom.

We addressed three questions: (1) how do different approaches capture translanguaging behaviour; (2) to what extent does reported home language use correspond to observed language use during narration; and (3) do these behaviours differ with child age?

text.text: The data analysed in the present study were drawn from the Talk Together Study (Woon et al., 2021), a pre-registered micro-longitudinal study investigating parental language use for Singaporean families with preschool children aged between 8 to 40 months.

text.text: The Talk Together Study includes a randomised controlled intervention designed to support caregivers in enhancing the quality and quantity of talk when interacting with their children (Styles, 2021).

text.text: Families were randomly assigned to either the intervention or control arm using a double-blind method.

Families in the intervention arm received text messages containing evidence-based tips and interactive content aimed at enhancing child-directed talk twice a day over four weeks (binte Amran et al., 2021; Sundaray et al., 2021).

text.text: Families in the control arm received less frequent, general information on child language development, as a kind of 'sham intervention' (Styles, 2021).

text.text: Following four weeks, families switched conditions, such that all families received the full set of intervention materials.
To evaluate whether the effects of intervention on parental speech, caregivers and their children were invited to complete a shared picturebook narration task.
The shared picturebook narration task was conducted remotely via Zoom video-conferencing software.
Caregivers gave consent for the video calls (including their child's voice) to be recorded using the Zoom videoconferencing recording function.
Participants were presented with the open-access wordless picture book "Little Orangutan: What a Scary Storm" (Styles, 2020).
text.formatted: Participants were presented with the open-access wordless picture book "Little Orangutan: What a Scary Storm" <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(Styles, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: As the picturebook did not contain any words, caregivers were free to describe the book's illustrations using any language or language mix typical for use with their child.
During the video call, the study researcher used Zoom's screensharing function to display the picture book two pages at a time, as shown in Figure 1.
text.formatted: During the video call, the study researcher used Zoom's screensharing function to display the picture book two pages at a time, as shown in Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref>.

text.text: Caregivers were instructed to say "next" when they were ready to proceed, after which the researcher displayed the following pages.
A jingling sound was played to signal each page turn.

As the current study is designed to explore the suitability of our proposed approaches for characterising caregiver translanguaging behaviours, the data analysed in this study uses only the recordings of the picturebook narration sessions completed in Timepoint 1, prior to exposure to the intervention.
This restriction ensured that the analysed speech represented caregivers' baseline language use and avoided potential effects of the intervention on their speech behaviours.
The Timepoint 1 corpus consists of a total of picturebook narrations from 146 parent-child dyads.
At Timepoint 1, children's ages ranged from 8 to 40 months (Median=1;6).

All audio recordings of narrations were transcribed in ELAN (Nijmegen: Max Planck Institute for Psycholinguistics) using a custom transcription protocol (BELA: Loh et al., 2022a;  https://blipntu.github.io/belacon/).

text.text: Video recordings were consulted when additional information was required for transcription.

The BELA transcription protocol uses a custom standardised transcription template in which each speaker in the recording was assigned a separate tier set comprising an Utterance tier, a Chunk tier, a Language tier, and a Translation tier.
Utterances were defined as vocal output produced by a speaker and utterance boundaries were determined primarily by intonation patterns and pauses (Loh et al., 2022b).
text.formatted: Utterances were defined as vocal output produced by a speaker and utterance boundaries were determined primarily by intonation patterns and pauses <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Loh et al., 2022b)</ref>.

text.text: Transcribers were instructed to place speaker-turn boundaries as precisely as possible, including sounds occurring at the edges of words, such as final fricatives.
In cases of overlapping speech, transcribers identified the onset and offset of each speaker's turn to the best of their judgement, resulting in individual timestamps per speaker.

text.text: Utterances are further subdivided into smaller 'chunks' to mark either a change in language or a transition between speech and non-linguistic communicative acts, such as humming or clapping.

Each chunk was assigned a label on a dedicated Language tier using a set of labels developed and refined iteratively, taking into account the languages commonly spoken in Singapore and those encountered in the study sample.

Speech chunks were assigned a corresponding language label (e.g., English, Mandarin, Malay, Tamil), while non-linguistic chunks were assigned a label according to the type of communicative act, e.g., vocal sounds such as humming and whistling versus non-vocal sounds such as clapping.
The full coding scheme is provided in Loh et al. (2022c).
text.formatted: The full coding scheme is provided in <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">Loh et al. (2022c)</ref>.

text.text: Non-English utterances were additionally provided with approximate English translations on the Translation tier.
Note.
Utterances are subdivided into chunks based on their language tags, and white spaces are placed between Mandarin words in the Chunk tier as outlined in the BELA transcription convention.

The BELA protocol also incorporated conventions to support consistent word-level segmentation across languages and enable the automatic extraction of word counts from the transcriptions (Loh et al., 2022b).
text.formatted: The BELA protocol also incorporated conventions to support consistent word-level segmentation across languages and enable the automatic extraction of word counts from the transcriptions <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Loh et al., 2022b)</ref>.

text.text: First, spaces were used to mark word boundaries in all languages, even when this convention differed from the language's conventional writing system (i.e., Mandarin Chinese).
Second, spelling was standardised across different pronunciations of the same lexeme to ensure consistent word-token counts.
For example, although the informal Singaporean of already is sometimes spelled oreddy in informal contexts (cf.
Gwee, 2017), the standard spelling already was used throughout the transcriptions.
Third, multi-part words conventionally written as separate words were hyphenated (e.g., choo-choo) to facilitate consistent word-boundary identification.
Together, these conventions enabled word counts to be extracted automatically from the transcriptions based on whitespacedelimited units.
Further discussion of the methodological decisions underlying multilingual transcription is provided in Choo et al. (2026).

text.text: Our set of language labels also included two special language labels: "Languageless" vocabulary and "Red-Dot" vocabulary.

Since filler speech and interjections such as 'um' and 'ah' can be used by speakers regardless of language backgrounds, in the Language tier, this speech was labelled 'Languageless' (i.e., lacking a specific language label; see Loh et al., 2022c for the full list of language tags).

text.text: The language tier labels 'Languageless' and 'Red Dot' were used to provide a language-model-neutral base dataset that could be analysed in a variety of different ways.
Rebadging.
In the current report, we are interested in comparing metrics that capture a speaker's deployment of their multilingual resources across linguistic varieties.

Since Languageless and Red Dot words do not constitute discrete language varieties (rather they can form a part of any utterances in any language), we rebadged Languageless and Red Dot chunks to coordinate with language of the surrounding speech, as follows: Clause-final Red Dot discourse markers were rebadged according to the language label of the preceding chunk.
When a Languageless or Red Dot chunk appeared at the beginning of an utterance, it was rebadged with the language label of the following named-language chunk.
When a Languageless or Red Dot chunk appeared at the end of an utterance, it was rebadged with the language label of the preceding named-language chunk.
When a Languageless or Red Dot chunk appeared between two chunks with the same named language label, it was rebadged with that language label.

When a Languageless or Red Dot chunk appeared between two chunks with different named language labels, it was rebadged with the label of the language that accounted for the greater cumulative duration within the utterance.

Finally, for utterances consisting entirely of Languageless or Red Dot chunks, all chunks in the utterance were rebadged with the language that was spoken for the longest duration by the speaker across the entire narration.
Figure 3 illustrates this rebadging procedure for Languageless and Red Dot chunks in our transcriptions.

text.text: After rebadging the special language labels (Languageless and Red-Dot), the languagelevel annotations of 146 picturebook narrations provided the basis for the present analyses, allowing language identity to be tracked across each narration and were used to derive our proposed approaches.
Reported home language use.
We used the Language Experience Overview (LEO; Woon et al., 2021) to capture caregivers' estimates of their children's multilingual experiences.
text.formatted: We used the Language Experience Overview (LEO; <ref type="bibr">Woon et al., 2021)</ref> to capture caregivers' estimates of their children's multilingual experiences.

text.text: For each family, one caregiver enrolled in the study completed the LEO survey, providing information about all individuals who cared for their child during waking hours on a typical weekday and weekend day.
The participating caregiver identified these individuals and estimated the proportion of time each individual used different linguistic varieties with the child.
For example, a single caregiver might be reported as using English 50% of the time, Mandarin 40% of the time, and Cantonese 10% of the time.
For three of the 146 caregiver-child dyads who took part in the narration task language-use was estimated by their partner.

As all families in the study reported English as one of the languages used in the home, we investigated the proportion of English use at home, expressed as a proportion ranging from 0 to 1, with higher values indicating greater English use.
We focused on English because it is the dominant language of education and early childhood care in Singapore.
Of the 146 caregiver-child dyads, we computed the reported proportion of English use at home for 144 caregivers, excluding two caregivers who did not complete the LEO survey.
To characterise the full range of diversity and balance of languages used at home, we also calculated home language entropy, which is reported in Supplement S1.
The rebadged transcriptions of the storybook narration were used as the basis of the observed measures of language use.
Hence, all metrics in the current report are computed on the basis of word-count and utterance counts, excluding non-speech chunks.

To enable an understanding of how long a parent speaks using resources from a single language before deploying resources from another language, we computed a 'span' of speech as a sequence of consecutive chunks assigned the same language label, including across utterance boundaries.
The lengths of a language span and a language chunk are measured as the number of words.

text.text: For each picturebook narration, we computed the proportion of English used as the total number of English words spoken over the total number of words spoken, expressed as a value ranging from 0 to 1 with higher values indicating a greater proportion of English use.
This metric allowed direct comparison with the reported home-language use proportions.

An utterance was classified as multilingual if it contained speech chunks assigned to at least two distinct language labels, and as monolingual if all speech chunks within the utterance were assigned the same language label.
For each picturebook narration, the proportion of multilingual utterances was calculated by dividing the number of multilingual utterances by the total number of speech-containing utterances.

Higher values indicate a greater proportion of caregiver utterances included more than one language during picturebook narration, whereas lower values indicate a greater proportion of utterances containing only one language.

Whereas their approach characterises individuals' language-use patterns using questionnaire data, our approach derives language-use proportions directly from processed speech transcripts.

text.text: As four different span lengths are observed, each occurring equally often, this caregiver would have the maximum possible entropy for four observed span-length categories (span entropy = 2).

Span entropy therefore provides a measure of how consistently or variably caregivers sustain their use of a given language across consecutive words before they use another language, irrespective of which languages were used.

Higher values indicate that language spans are distributed more evenly across a greater number of distinct length categories, whereas lower values indicate that language spans are concentrated in fewer length categories.
When all language spans have the same length or there is only one span (i.e., only one language used), span entropy is zero, reflecting the absence of variation in span lengths.

Memory ranges from -1 to 1.
Positive values mean that successive span lengths tend to deviate from their respective means in the same direction, so long spans tend to be followed by long spans and short by short.
Negative values mean that they deviate in opposite directions, so long spans tend to be followed by short ones.
Values near zero indicate little linear sequential dependence between successive span lengths.
For example, a caregiver with span lengths of [2, 3, 7, 8] would have a positive memory value, whereas a caregiver with span lengths of [2, 7, 3, 8] would have a negative memory value.

Although both caregivers produced the same set of span lengths, their sequential arrangements differ: in the first sequence, short spans follow short spans and long follow long, whereas in the second sequence, shorter and longer spans follow one another.
Thus, memory characterises the sequential organisation of language-span lengths, complementing span entropy, which characterises their distribution regardless of order.
Memory cannot be estimated reliably for speakers with fewer than three spans, because estimating a correlation between consecutive span lengths requires at least two pairs of consecutive spans.
This included all speakers who used only one language, each of whom produced a single span.

Memory was also undefined when span lengths showed no variation across consecutive-span pairs (e.g., when all spans consisted of the same number of words), because a correlation cannot be calculated when either variable has zero variance.

In these cases, memory was recorded as missing rather than zero, since a value of zero would indicate an absence of correlation between consecutive span lengths, rather than an inability to estimate it.
Although a correlation can be calculated for speakers with exactly three spans, it is based on only two pairs of consecutive spans.
With just two pairs, the correlation is necessarily either +1 or -1, provided neither variable has zero variance.

These extreme values arise from the mathematical constraints of the calculation and make it uninformative as an estimate of the strength of sequential dependence between consecutive language span lengths.
Accordingly, narrations with fewer than four spans, as well as narrations for which memory could not be estimated because of zero variance in span lengths, were excluded from analyses of memory.

What combinations of linguistic varieties do parents report using with their child at home?
One family did not complete the self-report, while another family completed the selfreport for only one caregiver, resulting in a total of 144 completed reports of caregiver's language use.
Almost all caregivers reported multilingual language use with their child (n = 127, 88%), with only a small proportion reporting monolingualism (n = 17, 12.0%).
Among multilingual families, 108 caregivers reported using two linguistic varieties with their child, 13 reported three linguistic varieties, and six reported four or five linguistic varieties.

Caregivers reported using a total of thirteen linguistic varieties with their child: English, Mandarin, Malay, Tamil, Hokkien, Cantonese, Teochew, Arabic, Hindi, Bahasa Indonesia, Spanish, Korean, and Burmese.
Of these, English was reported by 100% of the caregivers, followed by Mandarin (n = 102 caregivers, 70.8%), Malay (n = 14 caregivers, 9.72%) and Tamil (n = 8 caregivers, 5.56%).
The reported proportion of time caregivers used English with their child ranged from 5% to 100%.

text.text: What language combinations did caregivers report using with their child?

Among 127 caregivers who reported using multiple linguistic varieties with their child, the most common combination was English and Mandarin (n = 86), followed by English and Malay (n = 11) and English and Tamil (n = 8).

Other combinations were reported by smaller numbers of caregivers, with English paired with less frequently reported linguistic varieties, such as Bahasa Indonesia, Hindi, Burmese, Spanish, each reported by one caregiver.
A subset of caregivers used three or more linguistic varieties with their child (n = 18).

text.text: What linguistic varieties did parents use when narrating a picturebook to their child?

The majority of transcriptions included words from more than one linguistic variety (n = 88, 59.6%), with fewer narrations including words from only one linguistic variety (Englishonly: n = 58, 40.4%).
Among multilingual narrations, 81 included words from two linguistic varieties with their child, 6 included three linguistic varieties, and 1 included four linguistic varieties.
During the narration task, we observed a total of seven linguistic varieties used by caregivers: English, Mandarin, Malay, Tamil, Hokkien, Arabic, Hindi.

Of these, English was the most widely used, appearing in the narrations of all 146 caregivers (100%), followed by Mandarin (68 caregivers, 46.6%), Malay (15 caregivers, 10.3%), Tamil (6 caregivers, 4.11%), Arabic (5 caregivers, 3.42%), Hokkien (1 caregiver, 0.685%), Hindi (1 caregiver, 0.685%).
The observed proportion of English ranged from 5% to 100%.

text.text: Each row in the strip plot represents one narration, stacked in order of child age, and colour coded to represent linguistic varieties.
From the strip plot, we can observe that many caregivers use their linguistic resources together in spans that result in a complex weave.
While English is clearly the dominant language in the corpus, there is considerable variability in how linguistic varieties are distributed across narrations.

Whereas some narrations are predominantly produced in one linguistic variety, others contain substantial contributions from multiple linguistic varieties, highlighting individual differences in language use beyond the language combinations reported.

Moreover, the distribution of colours within individual narrations further illustrates that multilingual input is complex and variable: linguistic resources from different languages are deployed in stretches of varying lengths, producing distinct patterns of language use within and across narrations.

Do parental estimates of home language use align with their observed narration behaviour?

Of the 144 caregivers who completed both the language use report and the narration task, 79 caregivers used the same linguistic varieties during the narration task as those they reported using with their child.
Another 44 caregivers reported using multiple linguistic varieties with their child but were observed using only English during the narration task.
The remaining 21 caregivers showed varying degrees of difference between reported and observed language use.

Specifically, nine caregivers reported using linguistic varieties at home that were not observed during the narration task, five reported using only English with their child but used additional linguistic varieties during the task, four used more linguistic varieties during the narration task than they reported using at home with their child, and three showed partial overlap between reported and observed language use.

As all parents reported using English and all parents used English in their narrations, we investigated how the reported proportion of English used corresponded with the observed proportion of English used.

Children growing up with more than one language experience different linguistic environments and capturing this variability requires measures that treat multilingual experience as continuous (Kremin & Byers-Heinlein, 2021).

text.text: We examined how language-use visualizations, proportion of English use, language entropy, proportion of multilingual utterances, span entropy and memory, capture the unique ways caregivers distribute and combine their languages in speech.
Our findings suggest that these measures provide complementary information about different patterns of multilingualism, and we provide tools to compute them (doi.org/10.21979/N9/QKG3CQ).

There was moderate correspondence between reported and observed proportion of English (See Figure S1 for similar findings for language entropy), with notable differences between reported and observed language use, consistent with earlier work reporting variable agreement (e.g., Marchman et al., 2017; Cychosz et al., 2021).

text.text: Many parents used more English in the narration task than was reported used at home.
This discrepancy may be due to the nature of self-report or the narration task being different to the context of the home environment.
Previous research has shown that language use varies with interaction context and interlocutors (e.g., Tare & Felman, 2011).
text.formatted: Previous research has shown that language use varies with interaction context and interlocutors (e.g., <ref type="bibr">Tare & Felman, 2011)</ref>.

text.text: In our case, narrating a wordless picture book over Zoom, with an unfamiliar off-camera researcher present, likely elicited patterns that differed from everyday home interactions.
These discrepancies indicate that reported and observed speech may index different aspects of child language input.
Our measures of observed language in narrations capture different aspects of how multilingual speech is structured.

English was reported by all caregivers and observed in every narration, with 40.4% conducted entirely in English, consistent with the status of English as the primary language of education and governance in Singapore.
Previous research has questioned whether multiple languages within an utterance hinder or support language learning (see Kaushanskaya, 2023, for a review).
text.formatted: Previous research has questioned whether multiple languages within an utterance hinder or support language learning (see <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Kaushanskaya, 2023</ref>, for a review).

text.text: Some evidence suggests naturalistic mixing shapes learning (Adamou & Shen, 2019), and with repetition, does not impair novel word learning (Kaushanskaya et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Some evidence suggests naturalistic mixing shapes learning <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Adamou & Shen, 2019)</ref>, and with repetition, does not impair novel word learning <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Kaushanskaya et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: In our study, 55% of the caregivers use multilingual utterances at least once (2.4% of utterances were translanguaged), showing that within-utterance mixing is part of Singaporean children's input.

Given the high prevalence of English in our dataset, proportions of English can serve as a baseline metric for all caregivers, however it does not capture how language use might be balanced across different numbers of languages.
We observed declining language entropy with child age, suggesting parents tended towards one language with older children.
One advantage of language entropy is that it can be used when no common language exists among speakers within a dataset, making it language neutral.
As entropy does not identify which language(s) are used most, it is best interpreted alongside language proportions and the number of languages spoken.
Span entropy and memory characterise the unfolding of language sequences over time.

Experimental work has suggested that abrupt language changes may carry short-lived costs for novel word learning (Libersky et al., 2024), while repeated exposure may enhance learning (Kaushanskaya et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Experimental work has suggested that abrupt language changes may carry short-lived costs for novel word learning <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Libersky et al., 2024)</ref>, while repeated exposure may enhance learning <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Kaushanskaya et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: In this paper, we applied these metrics at one time point to characterise caregiver language behaviour, but links to developmental outcomes remain to be tested.

The same span entropy value may reflect mostly short spans for one caregiver and mostly long spans for another (see Supplement S2), hence span entropy is best interpreted alongside span-length proportions and the number of spans.
text.formatted: The same span entropy value may reflect mostly short spans for one caregiver and mostly long spans for another (see Supplement <ref type="table" target="#tab_1">S2</ref>), hence span entropy is best interpreted alongside span-length proportions and the number of spans.

text.text: Memory is undefined for narrations with fewer spans, making it best suited to datasets with longer tasks, multiple time points, or samples where multilingual use is common.
In exploratory, cross-sectional analyses, age-related variation was evident in language distribution.

Among multilingual narrations, caregivers of older children seemed to use their repertoires less evenly and used proportionally more English, with no differences in utterancelevel mixing or span organisation.
Longitudinal research is needed to determine whether this reflects change within families or differences between families.
Measures that depend on segmentation and labelling require careful decisions, which are consequential where language boundaries are not straightforward, as in Singapore (Lee, 2003; Ong et al., 2013).

text.text: Our transcriptions were designed to be language-model neutral, allowing analysis under models such as code-switching among discrete named-languages, or more flexible approaches like translanguaging.

The current analysis took a permissive approach, rebadging specially labelled items (Languageless and Red Dot) according to the language labels of their nearest neighbours, or most frequently spoken languages.
Hence 'wah' could be considered English in the utterance "Wah, look", or Malay in "Wah tiba-tiba" (see
Figure 3).
text.formatted: Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">3</ref>).

text.text: This is an operational solution, not a definitive account of boundaries between linguistic varieties, and other approaches may be better suited to other communities or research questions.
Rebadging affects span boundaries and utterance classifications, so span entropy, memory and proportion of multilingual utterances are most affected.
Thus, comparison of the current study with others should take careful consideration of the language models underlying the data.
Since each metric highlights a different feature of multilingual language resource deployment, exploratory analyses are valuable for understanding complex dynamics of language use.
We make available our code for rebadging, analysing and visualising multilingual data in this article's repository.
The code is optimised for BELA transcripts, which use whitespace to delineate word boundaries, but includes an option to compute metrics using time-stamps rather than word counts.

To avoid inflated experimenter degrees of freedom, selection of metrics for hypothesis testing should be justified by the research question: proportions of language-use for relative exposure, language entropy for balance, proportion of multilingual utterances for within-utterance translanguaging, and span entropy and memory for span organisation.

By describing multilingual input with continuous measures, our report and code repository aims to help researchers characterise variability within multilingual groups rather than treating them as homogeneous.
In this study, all observed measures were computed from one picturebook narration, so we cannot establish whether patterns generalise across activities or vary over time.

Future research could apply these measures across contexts, communities and timepoints, and test whether the measures explain variation in language, vocabulary, communicative or pragmatic outcomes beyond exposure proportions, for example in designs that consider child age and caregiver proficiency.

This study demonstrates how different complementary measures (language-use visualization plots, language-use proportions, language entropy, proportion of multilingual utterances, span entropy, and memory) can characterise distinct aspects of multilingual speech.

Together, these measures capture the amount of languages used, how evenly languages are distributed across a caregiver's repertoire, whether multiple languages occur within individual utterances, how much language-span lengths vary, and the extent to which successive spans are related.
Rather than proposing a single comprehensive index of multilingual input, our report provides a foundation for investigating different dimensions of caregiver translanguaging.

text.text: The caregiver with a span entropy closest to the sample median distributed spans across approximately 10 length categories, with each span length category accounting for around 10% of spans.

The caregiver with the lowest entropy produced spans concentrated in three length categories, each accounting for approximately 33% of spans, indicating that they tended to sustain their use of English or Mandarin for a narrower range of consecutive-word lengths.

In contrast, the caregiver with the highest entropy distributed spans across a greater number of length categories (n = 28), with most length categories accounting for no more than approximately 5% of spans, indicating greater diversity in how long they sustained each language before changing to another language.
As span entropy is calculated from the distribution of observed span lengths, its estimation depends on both the number of spans produced and the number of length categories.
Figure S2.2 shows the relationship between the total number of language spans and span entropy across caregivers.
text.formatted: Figure <ref type="figure">S2</ref>.2 shows the relationship between the total number of language spans and span entropy across caregivers.

text.text: Span entropy increased more rapidly across lower span counts, whereas the relationship became more gradual at higher span counts.
In addition, entropy values were more widely dispersed among caregivers with fewer spans, while the range of values was narrower among caregivers with more spans, although some variation remained.
When fewer spans are observed, individual spans may have a greater influence on the estimated distribution of span length, potentially contributing to greater variability in entropy estimates.
At the same time, the observed dispersion may reflect genuine differences in caregivers' spanlength distributions.

Thus, this pattern highlights the importance of considering the amount of language data available when comparing span entropy across caregivers, as the observed relationship may reflect both differences in span-length distributions and variability associated with the amount of data available.

Worked Example of Memory Figure S3.1 illustrates the sequential organisation of language-span lengths in three caregivers' narrations with at least 10 language spans: the caregivers with a negative memory score, a positive memory score, and a memory score closest to the sample median.
text.formatted: Worked Example of Memory Figure <ref type="figure">S3</ref>.1 illustrates the sequential organisation of language-span lengths in three caregivers' narrations with at least 10 language spans: the caregivers with a negative memory score, a positive memory score, and a memory score closest to the sample median.

text.text: The negative median memory score across caregivers indicated a slight tendency for caregivers to produce shorter stretches in one language following longer stretches, and vice versa.
This characteristic is reflected more strongly in the caregiver with a higher negative memory score.
At the start of the narration, the caregiver used very short Mandarin spans of 1 to 5 words with longer English spans of more than 10 words.
As they continued with the narration task, the caregiver appeared to use very short English spans of 1 to 2 words with longer Mandarin spans of more than 20 words.
In contrast, the caregiver with a positive, albeit low, memory score showed a slight tendency for successive language spans to have similar relative lengths.
For instance, at the start of the narration task, they tended to follow a long English span with another long Mandarin span.
Towards the end of the narration task, they tended to produce short English and Mandarin spans.
These contrasting examples illustrate how memory captures the sequential organisation of word counts across stretches of languages used.
To explore these differences in greater detail, Table S4.1 compares four narrations that receive similar scores on one metric but different scores on another.

text.text: Caregivers A (English-Mandarin) and B (English-Tamil) had similar language entropy scores but differed in the proportion of words produced in English: 87.1% of Caregiver A's words were produced in English, compared with 13% for Caregiver B. As language entropy captures the distribution of language use without indicating which language predominates, similar entropy scores can occur even when the relative use of each language differs substantially.
Examining language entropy alongside language proportions therefore provides a more complete picture of caregivers' language use.
Caregivers A and B also differed in the extent to which they used multiple languages within individual utterances.
Approximately 2.23% of Caregiver A's utterances contained both English and Mandarin, compared with 18.3% of Caregiver B's utterances containing both English and Tamil (Table S4.1).
text.formatted: Approximately 2.23% of Caregiver A's utterances contained both English and Mandarin, compared with 18.3% of Caregiver B's utterances containing both English and Tamil (Table <ref type="table">S4</ref>.1).

text.text: This suggests that similar levels of language entropy can coexist with different patterns of language mixing, particularly in the extent to which languages are combined within utterances.

For Caregiver A, the low proportion of multilingual utterances suggests that language use was more often distributed across utterances, although this does not necessarily establish that languages alternated between consecutive utterances.

These differences illustrate how narrations with similar language entropy can differ both in the relative use of a particular language and in how frequently languages are combined within an utterance.

Caregivers B (English-Tamil) and C (English-Mandarin) had similar language proportions, language entropy scores, and memory estimates, but differed in their use of multiple languages within utterances and in span entropy scores (Table S4.1).

text.text: Within individual utterances, caregiver B combined English and Tamil more frequently (18.3%) than caregiver C combined English and Mandarin (10.3%).
